extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, judges, agency policymakers, and researchers working on algorithmic decision-making and notice-and-comment issues
extracted.subtask_description: Framework for determining when an agency's algorithmic system should be treated as a binding 'rule' (triggering notice-and-comment) versus nonbinding 'guidance', drawing on administrative-law tests, Bayesian persuasion, and HCI evidence about human–algorithm interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practically binding test
rubrics_metrics.description: A document can be binding either because (1) agencies themselves expect the document to be binding on adjudicators and say so, or (2) because it appears to have the effect of binding adjudicators in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts use both ex ante and ex post evidence to apply this test; the inquiry is functional and aims to capture how the document is used within the agency. (Levin; Appalachian Power discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory language / regular application on face of document
rubrics_metrics.description: If the document is 'couched in mandatory language, or in terms indicating that it will be regularly applied,' it is more likely a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual indicators (e.g., mandatory verbs, prescriptive phrasing) can be sufficient to render a document binding as a practical matter (citing General Elec. Co. v. EPA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive effect / grave consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the substantive effect of the document is 'sufficiently grave' — i.e., has important real-world distributive consequences — increases the likelihood courts will deem it a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies with major distributive impacts are more apt to require notice-and-comment; courts sometimes weigh gravity of effects alongside textual indicators (citing Elec. Priv. Info. Ctr.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex post practical bindingness (agency conduct and downstream reliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A document is more likely a rule if the agency 'acts as if a document issued at headquarters is controlling in the field,' if it 'leads private parties' or other government entities to believe they must comply, or if it 'bases enforcement actions on the policies or interpretations formulated in the document.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex post evidence of how agencies actually apply the document (conduct, enforcement reliance, private parties' behavior) can convert facially nonbinding language into a practically binding rule (citing Appalachian Power Co. v. EPA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of routine departure from policy
rubrics_metrics.description: If agency adjudicators exhibit practical evidence of regularly departing from the department’s policy, the document is more likely to be treated as guidance despite mandatory-sounding language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look to operational flexibility shown in agency behavior; consistent departures support nonbinding classification (citing Sierra Club v. EPA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heckler v. Chaney prosecutorial-discretion carve-out
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents that bind officials in the exercise of enforcement (prosecutorial) discretion are typically shielded from notice-and-comment under Heckler v. Chaney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a result, algorithms used primarily for enforcement may be largely exempt from notice-and-comment scrutiny, though recent cases (e.g., Texas) complicate the doctrine and circuits vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of large distributive consequences and use for enforcement/adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Two key factors identified by Engstrom & Ho: (1) presence of large distributive consequences, and (2) use of the algorithm for enforcement or adjudication — both increase the case for treating an algorithm as a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors are normatively relevant and have strong doctrinal significance in distinguishing rulelike algorithmic systems from mere guidance; they are not alone always dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine exercise of human discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether humans retain a 'genuine exercise of human discretion' when using the algorithmic system — a contested but central doctrinal question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article treats this as the linchpin question and seeks to give it content by connecting it to an operationalizable notion (see next entries). Engstrom & Ho emphasize this factor in their guidance/rule framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion defined as effortful updating (operational definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discretion is defined as 'adding to [one's] set of prior beliefs by expending effort to perceive, gather, or interpret information about a given case' — i.e., effortful updating of priors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this account, an adjudicator exercises discretion when she integrates algorithm outputs with independent fact-finding or interpretation (e.g., holistically assessing circumstances); failing to do so (e.g., always deferring to algorithm's uniform rule) indicates lack of discretion and pushes toward 'rule' classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bayesian persuasion / information-design risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms can act as 'senders' that design signals to persuade 'receivers' (line adjudicators), influencing how humans update priors and thereby biasing decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying Bayesian persuasion concepts helps predict when algorithmic presentation will be highly persuasive; courts should consider the persuasive power of signal design (order, strength, framing) when assessing practical bindingness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automation bias and HCI-derived cognitive vulnerabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Human-computer interaction evidence documents cognitive biases — e.g., automation bias, selective adherence — that make humans overestimate or selectively follow algorithmic predictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HCI studies identify interface and design features that amplify deference; these empirical facts bear on whether a purportedly nonbinding algorithm will be practically binding in application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal structure: recommendation scope (final disposition vs subcomponent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the algorithm outputs a recommendation for the final disposition (e.g., suggested bail amount) versus a recommendation on a subcomponent (e.g., which evidence to consult) matters for persuasiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct recommendations about ultimate outcomes are more likely to induce compliance; courts should consider the kind of signal produced when evaluating binding effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease of access to auxiliary evidence (capacity to evaluate algorithm)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which an adjudicator can easily access auxiliary evidence against which the algorithm’s prediction may be evaluated affects likelihood of deference: the easier the access, the less likely the adjudicator will defer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Auxiliary evidence includes factual records or other data the adjudicator could consult; if such evidence is hard to obtain or interpret, algorithmic recommendations become comparatively more persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex ante versus ex post evidentiary approaches and circuit variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts use both ex ante (textual indicators like mandatory language) and ex post (implementation and effects) approaches, and circuit emphasis varies — some favor functionalist analysis, others require a combination of factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of heterogeneity across circuits and difficulty of retrospective causal inference, reliance on ex post empirical data is often challenging without systematic agency data collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-implementation and midstream audits / independent oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: System-level oversight interventions such as pre-implementation or midstream audits can identify unexpected harms and assess algorithms' fit with policy objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audits (internal or third-party) and new oversight bodies are proposed mechanisms to detect and mitigate biases and to provide information useful to courts and regulators evaluating bindingness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Randomization / benchmarking to permit impact comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring randomization when agencies implement algorithmic tools permits comparisons between decisions made with and without the tool (benchmarking relative to a random hold-out set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randomized comparisons allow decision-makers and courts to 'smoke out' inaccuracies and biases in real time and produce ex post evidence about an algorithm's practical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procurement-based transparency guarantees and trade-secret waivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporating guarantees of 'conform[ance] to specified standards for ethical AI' and 'limited waivers of trade secret and other intellectual property protections' into public procurement can ensure transparency of contractor-supplied algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procurement reforms (including contractual inspection/audit rights and IP waiver rules) are a practical way for agencies to obtain necessary information to evaluate algorithmic tools and to reduce opacity concerns.
